text: Keep everything forever and delete everything fast are both failure modes. Data retention is the deliberate practice of deciding, in advance and by data category, how long something is kept and what happens to it afterward. This chapter picks up right after classification and access control, because you can't set a sensible retention period for data you haven't identified.

Over-retention feels safe, we might need it someday, but every extra year of customer records sitting in a database is another year it can be breached, another year it must be secured, another year someone has to honor an erasure request against it. Under-retention is the opposite failure, deleting records before a legal or contractual obligation to keep them has expired, which creates an audit finding, not efficiency. It also breaks legal holds, when litigation is reasonably anticipated, normal retention schedules get suspended, and deleting data on schedule anyway can look like destroying evidence.

A usable retention schedule answers four questions for every data category. Category, what kind of data this is. Retention period, stated as a duration, not a vague as needed. Trigger event, what starts the clock, a contract end date, an account closure, a fiscal year end, retention periods rarely start at creation. Disposition action, what happens when the period ends, secure deletion, anonymization, or transfer to archive.

Skipping the trigger event is the most common mistake. Seven years means nothing without a starting point, seven years from when the record was created versus seven years from when the relationship ended produces very different deletion dates for a customer who stayed ten years.
Classification tells you which rule applies, retention tells you how long the clock runs. Next up: data deletion and the right to erasure, what disposition actually looks like when someone asks.
